newsitem.title: USA: US debt futures end up, Dec bonds above 7-mth high.
newsitem.headline: US debt futures end up, Dec bonds above 7-mth high.

text.p: U.S. debt futures finished sharply higher, as the market priced out any chance of a U.S. interest rate rate hike this year, traders and analysts said.
"The feeling that the Fed will hike rates in November -- it's done with, it's over," one Eurodollar trader said.
December T-bonds USZ6 stretched gains throughout the afternoon after a decline in the U.S. October consumer confidence index sent the contract barreling through the seven-month high of 111-28/32.
"We are going to build from here," a trader said about the lack of resistance points at these high levels.
The confidence index fell to 106.2, versus average trade estimates of 111.6. It was the third major U.S. economic number this morning that showed the pace of growth was slowing.
"Confidence is now waning as economic momentum failed to carry through the fall," Brian Wesbury, vice president and chief economist at Griffin, Kubik, Stephens & Thompson Inc, said in a newsletter.

He said a surge in jobs growth in the second quarter and in overall economic activity in the spring had driven consumer confidence higher. Within seconds of consumer confidence, December bonds soared through 112-02/32.

The 112-02/32 level corresponds to a cash bond yield of 6.75 percent. Bonds continued their ascent in the afternoon, with December rising to 112-22/32, despite Richmond Federal Reserve president Alfred Broaddus's comments.

Broaddus, who will vote on the Federal Open Market Committee in 1997, said U.S. economic policy was at a "crucial juncture." He said the economy was operating at a high level of activity, and that employment had been growing in a range that in the past has been associated with rising inflationary pressures.
The 112-23/32 level is a 50-percent retracement from the 9-1/2-month downmove.

Broaddus's statement that the U.S. needs to be concerned that so much recent growth has been financed from abroad did not make a dent in a market that has recently generated an enormous amount of buying interest from foreign central banks.
Traders and analysts said the smaller than expected increase in the U.S. third-quarter employment cost index erased concerns of wage-price inflation.

The index rose 0.6 percent, versus the average estimate of 0.8 percent. Wesbury noted that the employment cost index's rise of 2.8 percent year-on-year was lower than the consumer price index's gain of 2.9 percent in the same period.
